title: Can pruning too hard kill or harm my rose?

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: The view that pruning does not kill a rose is expert opinion, not measured (AF-1). One commercial website disagrees, saying cutting back too far "could stress it out or even kill it" (AF-20, Very Low; C-1). Sources disagree on whether "weak" means the whole plant or a single shoot (C-2), and on renovating in one go or in stages (C-4). Newly planted roses are outside this record.

content.heading: Can pruning too hard kill or harm my rose?

items.text: Rose societies, rose growers and a botanic garden in New Zealand, Australia, the UK and the US say pruning, even hard or badly done, doesn't kill an established rose.
Some of them add conditions: the rose is otherwise healthy, it isn't cut below the ground line, and its roots are intact.
The cut sources say can lose a rose is one made below the graft or below the ground line.
A weak or slow-growing rose is pruned less hard than a vigorous one. Within a bush, sources still cut single weak shoots back further or remove them.
Pruning before the frosts have passed risks frost damage to the new growth and dieback.
Sources describe any harm from pruning too hard as a short-term setback. One says the first year after a hard pruning is a recovery year.
An old or neglected rose can be brought back with hard pruning.
Pip's approach to a heavy renovation is to spread it over two or three years, about a third at a time. Some sources do it all in one go, and none gives a rule for choosing.
Sources give no signs or waiting time for judging recovery. If no new growth appears during the growing season, ask your local rose society.
